source.title: Selected results and open problems in a semiclassical theory of dense matter

accepted.question_text: In the Savic-Kasanin (SK) semiclassical theory of dense matter, the mean density rho of a planetary body is related to the mean solar density rho_0 by rho = rho_0 2^phi. A modern re-check using densities of 22 planets and major satellites reportedly still supports this relation, but now with non-integral values of the exponent phi for some objects. What physical interpretation, if any, should be assigned to these non-integral values of phi, and can they be explained by a principled extension of the earlier interpretation that treated integral phi values as a qualitative analogy to atomic quantization and pressure-induced changes in atomic structure?

evidence.quote: It was shown that eq.(1) is still valid,but that the exponent phi can also take non-integral values. The immediate question is of course the interpretation of these non-integral values.

accepted.question_text: The SK theory currently yields, for a celestial object, only a physically allowed interval for the angular speed of rotation rather than a single predicted value. What additional theoretical structure, constraints, or calculational procedure would allow the theory to determine a unique angular speed of rotation for a given celestial object, instead of only an admissible interval?

evidence.quote: Another "‘open"’ astronomical application of the SK theory is the calculation of the angular speed of rotation of a celestial object. Instead of proposing an algorithm for this calculation and giving a unique number at the end,this theory gives a physically allowed interval in which the speed of rotation can be. It was applied to the Earth and several other planets. The results are very promising,but it would be useful to reduce this allowed interval to a unique number.

accepted.question_text: For first-order phase transitions in compressed solids, discrepancies between phase-transition pressures predicted by the SK theory and experimentally measured pressures are reported to depend on both the material and the pressure range. If the theory is applied to a broader set of materials with known first-order phase-transition pressures, do systematic trends emerge in these discrepancies, and can such trends be characterized empirically well enough to reveal where the theory succeeds and where it fails?

evidence.quote: At first it would be useful to apply the theory to more materials for which first order phase transition presssures are known.In this way one would obtain a more precise empirical estimate of the systematic trends (if there are any) in the discrepancies between the calculated and measured values of the phase transition pressure.

accepted.question_text: The current SK theory explains phase-transition pressures using only a simplified electrostatic interaction and neglects additional contributions to the intermolecular or interparticle potential energy. How should the theory be refined so that more components of the interparticle potential energy are included, and does incorporating those missing potential terms materially reduce the discrepancy between predicted and measured high-pressure phase-transition pressures?

evidence.quote: the second "source of problems" is represented by the fact that the SK theory neglects the contribution of various non-electrostatic components to the overall intermolecular potential.
On the purely theoretical side,in would be necessary to refine the theory with the inclusion of the contribution of more components to the interparticle potential energy.

accepted.question_text: Although the SK semiclassical theory has produced useful numerical results, its formulation is described as unusual and this is presented as an obstacle to broader uptake. Can the SK theory be placed within the established framework of statistical physics by giving a systematic correspondence between its parameters and standard statistical-physics variables, so that the theory is no longer an isolated formalism but a special or derived case within a recognized framework?
accepted.context_brief: Linking SK theory to statistical physics

evidence.quote: An even more interesting problem would be to link the SK theory to the well established theoretical framework of statistical physics.Although the SK theory has given good results in a range of applications,its unusal formulation hinders its wider spread in the research community.

accepted.question_text: A preliminary comparison is said to connect parameters of the SK theory with those of Landau theory. Can the SK theory be reformulated in terms of modern theories of quantum phase transitions, so that its phase structure, control parameters, and predicted transitions are expressed using the language and methods of contemporary quantum critical phenomena rather than the original semiclassical presentation?

evidence.quote: A preliminary attempt in that direction has recently been performed in [21],where is was shown how the parameters appearing in the SK theory can be connected with those of the Landau theory. It would be interesting trying to reformulate the SK theory along the lines of present day theories of quantum phase transitions

accepted.question_text: The proposed thermal equation of state for solids in the temperature-density plane was derived using the Bohm-Staver approximation for the equation of state through the sound speed. If that calculation is repeated with a more refined and physically accurate equation of state, how does the resulting thermal equation of state change, and does the improved treatment preserve the physically acceptable numerical values obtained in the original derivation?
accepted.context_brief: Improving the thermal equation of state

evidence.quote: In the calculation which has led to the proposed form of thermal equation of state,an approximation called the "‘Bohm-Staver"’ formula was used [23].It is planned in the future to repeat this calculation,but using some more refined form of the equation of state.

accepted.question_text: Under static compression, metallic hydrogen had been predicted by the SK theory to appear near 300 GPa, but experiments up to 342 GPa had not shown metallization at the time of this paper, and disorder was suggested as one possible explanation for the mismatch. At what pressure and under what physical conditions, if any, does hydrogen actually undergo metallization under high pressure, and why had the experimentally accessible static-compression regime up to 342 GPa not yet exhibited the metallization expected from theory?

evidence.quote: Static experiments performed at values of pressure P ≤ 342 GPa have not shown signs of metallization of hydrogen [12],so the problem seems (at present)to be completely open.
